inputs.original_text: This is exactly how global crises deepen inequality: households and workers are made to absorb higher costs, while people with the most wealth and power are better placed to ride them out. Cutting fuel duties may offer temporary relief, but if the lost revenue is later recovered through weaker public services or other burdens on ordinary people, that is not a fair solution. India’s dependence on imported crude leaves people vulnerable to shocks they did not cause. We need a just, resilient energy transition that protects workers and low-income households instead of repeatedly asking them to pay the price.
inputs.modified_text: The real issue is who gets protected when energy prices spike. Workers and low-income households shouldn’t be left carrying the costs of a crisis they didn’t create, while the wealthy are better positioned to absorb the shock. Cutting fuel duties may help briefly, but it isn’t justice if the bill later comes through weaker public services or other burdens on ordinary people. India’s dependence on imported crude makes the need for a fair, resilient energy transition even more urgent—one that protects livelihoods and makes those with the greatest resources contribute fairly.
